title: Projects, Stacks and State
text:
Projects, Stacks and State
Every Pulumi command you run answers three questions before it touches a cloud API: which program (the project), which copy of it (the stack), and where is the record of what already exists (the backend and its state). Get those three straight and the rest of Pulumi is “write a program that declares resources”. Get them wrong and you deploy staging’s code into production’s state.

title: Projects, Stacks and State
text:
Learning goals

Read a Pulumi.yaml and say which runtime and entrypoint it selects
Create, select, rename and remove stacks, and explain fully qualified stack names
Export stack outputs and consume them from another project with a StackReference
Choose between Pulumi Cloud and a DIY backend, and know what pulumi refresh does and does not do




Two projects, three stacks each, linked by stack references; every stack has its own state in the backend.

title: Projects, Stacks and State
section: Projects: the program and its Pulumi.yaml
text:
Projects: the program and its Pulumi.yaml
A project is any directory containing a Pulumi.yaml. At run time Pulumi walks up from the current directory to the nearest one, and that file decides the project. pulumi new creates it.
name: webserver
runtime: python
description: A minimal Pulumi program.

name is the project name. It also namespaces configuration keys (next chapter).
runtime is one of nodejs, python, go, dotnet, java, yaml or hcl.
Each runtime finds its entrypoint by its own convention: __main__.py (or setup.py) for Python, package.json for Node, the build tool for Go, .NET and Java, .tf files for HCL.

The file name must start with a capital P. Either .yaml or .yml works.
For compiled languages you can skip the build at deploy time by pointing at a prebuilt binary:
name: my-project
runtime:
  name: go
  options:
    binary: mybinary
Paths. File paths inside a program are relative to the working directory. If the program must find files next to Pulumi.yaml regardless of where it was launched, use pulumi.get_root_directory() and convert the result to a path relative to the working directory, so plans don’t differ between machines.

title: Projects, Stacks and State
section: Stacks: many instances of one program
text:
Stacks: many instances of one program
A stack is an isolated, independently configured instance of the project’s program, typically dev, staging, production, or one per feature branch. Each stack has its own configuration and its own state. The program is shared.
pulumi stack init staging     # create and select
pulumi stack ls               # list stacks of the nearest project
pulumi stack select dev       # change the active stack
pulumi stack                  # show the active stack's resources and outputs
The commands config, preview, up and destroy act on the active stack. Pass --stack (or -s) in scripts and pipelines rather than relying on whatever was selected last.

Names
Stack names may contain letters, digits, hyphens, underscores and periods, and must be unique within a project. A stack can be written three ways:



Form
Meaning




dev
Current user or default organization, nearest project


acme/dev
Organization acme, nearest project


acme/webserver/dev
Fully qualified: organization, project, stack



On a DIY backend the organization part is always the literal organization. Backends initialised by a CLI older than v3.61.0 only understand the short form until upgraded with pulumi state upgrade.


Renaming has consequences
pulumi stack rename production changes the value of pulumi.get_stack(). If your program uses the stack name in resource names, the next pulumi up proposes replacements. Read the preview. Sometimes creating a new stack is the safer operation.
A rename across projects (acme/old-project/prod to acme/new-project/prod) needs two manual follow-ups: change name in Pulumi.yaml, and rename project-namespaced keys in Pulumi.<stack>.yaml (for example old-project:database to new-project:database). Skip the second step and the program silently sees those values as unset.


Removing
pulumi destroy deletes the stack’s resources. pulumi stack rm then deletes the empty stack, its history and its Pulumi.<stack>.yaml. pulumi stack rm --force removes a stack that still has resources, orphaning them. Do not.

title: Projects, Stacks and State
text:
Outputs: what a stack publishes
A stack exports values from the top level of the program:
import pulumi

pulumi.export("x", "hello")
pulumi.export("o", {"num": 42})
From the documentation (not run here), reading them back looks like:
$ pulumi stack output x
hello
$ pulumi stack output --json
{
  "x": "hello",
  "o": {
      "num": 42
  }
}
Outputs are effectively JSON-serialised and resolved after the update finishes. Export IDs and names, not whole resource objects, which serialise to large blobs. Secret outputs display as [secret] unless you pass --show-secrets.

title: Projects, Stacks and State
text:
Stack references: wiring projects together
Large systems split into projects by lifecycle and ownership, for example infra (network, cluster) and services (apps deployed onto it). The pairing is by environment: acme/infra/production feeds acme/services/production. A StackReference reads another stack’s outputs:
import pulumi
from pulumi import StackReference

env = pulumi.get_stack()
infra = StackReference(f"acme/infra/{env}")

kubeconfig = infra.require_output("kubeConfig")
Use the fully qualified name. Pulumi records the dependency between stacks. Choose the reader carefully:








Method
Behaviour
Use




require_output
Fails the deployment if the output is missing
Default choice; turns a typo into an error


get_output
Returns an output wrapping None if missing
Only when absence is expected and handled


get_output_details
Awaitable; returns .value or .secret_value directly
When program logic needs the raw value. Python needs an async entrypoint and SDK 3.254.0 or later



The referenced stack’s outputs are its public interface. Renaming an output is a breaking change for every consumer, just like renaming a function.

title: Projects, Stacks and State
text:
State and backends
Each stack’s state is Pulumi’s record of the resources it manages. preview and up diff the program against that record, not against the live cloud. The state lives in a backend:

Pulumi Cloud (the default, also self-hostable): pulumi login with no argument. Updates go through a transactional API with full history.
DIY: object storage you run (S3 or compatible such as MinIO or Ceph, Azure Blob, GCS), a PostgreSQL database, or the local filesystem. pulumi login <backend-url>, for example pulumi login file://~ for local files.

Avoid typing the URL every time by setting PULUMI_BACKEND_URL or a backend.url in Pulumi.yaml. pulumi whoami -v shows the user and the backend in use. Credentials for backends are stored in ~/.pulumi/credentials.json. Your cloud credentials are never stored in state. They stay where the CLI runs.
With a DIY backend you take on access control, encryption at rest, backups and auditing yourself. Checkpoint history lives under .pulumi/history/, but blob storage is not transactional, so some partial failures cannot be recovered automatically the way Pulumi Cloud recovers them.
Moving a stack between backends is pulumi stack migrate (CLI v3.254.0 or later). Log in to the target and name the source:
pulumi login                          # target: Pulumi Cloud
pulumi stack migrate file://~ my-app-production
It copies the latest checkpoint and configuration, re-encrypts secrets with the target’s secrets provider, and leaves the source untouched.

Drift and refresh
Pulumi does not query every resource on every run. That is a deliberate choice for speed, predictability and explicit control. A console edit is invisible until you run:
pulumi refresh              # update state from the cloud; changes no infrastructure
pulumi preview --refresh    # refresh, then show what up would do
pulumi up --refresh         # refresh, then converge to the program
After a refresh, the next up reverts out-of-band changes unless you also change the program to keep them.


Raw state
pulumi stack export --file stack.json and pulumi stack import --file stack.json give you the JSON checkpoint for inspection or emergency repair. An incorrect import can orphan resources. Export first, keep the copy, and prefer the pulumi state subcommands for targeted edits.

title: Projects, Stacks and State
text:
Diagnosis








Symptom
Likely cause
Check




up acts on the wrong environment
Active stack was not the one you assumed
pulumi stack ls (the * marks the active one); pass --stack


CLI says no project (Pulumi.yaml) was found
Running outside the project tree
ls Pulumi.yaml in the directory or a parent


Preview proposes replacing everything after a rename
Stack name used in resource names
Revert the rename, or accept replacement deliberately


Config values silently missing after rename
Project-namespaced keys still carry the old name
Inspect Pulumi.<stack>.yaml


StackReference fails
Wrong qualified name, missing permission, or output not exported
pulumi stack output -s org/project/stack


Stacks “disappeared”
Logged in to a different backend
pulumi whoami -v


Plan ignores a console change
No refresh
pulumi preview --refresh

title: Projects, Stacks and State
text:
Operational care

One project per lifecycle and owner. One stack per environment. Do not encode environments as if statements on the stack name for anything bigger than sizes and counts.
Commit Pulumi.yaml and the Pulumi.<stack>.yaml files of long-lived stacks (secrets in them are encrypted). Ephemeral stacks usually do not commit theirs.
In CI, always pass --stack with the fully qualified name, and run preview in pull requests and up on merge.
Tag stacks (pulumi stack tag set environment production) so Pulumi Cloud can group them. Avoid the reserved prefixes pulumi:, gitHub: and vcs:.
On DIY backends: version the bucket, restrict who can write, and back it up. That bucket is your inventory.

title: Projects, Stacks and State
text:
Practice

Sketch the project and stack layout for a system with a shared network, a database, and three services, across dev and production. How many stacks, and which references?
Write the StackReference line a services program needs to read vpcId from the matching infra stack, and justify require_output over get_output.
List what you must do yourself if you choose an S3 DIY backend instead of Pulumi Cloud.

title: Projects, Stacks and State
text:
Recall card

Project = directory with Pulumi.yaml (name, runtime). Stack = one configured instance with its own state.
org/project/stack is the full name. DIY backends use the literal organization.
pulumi.export publishes; StackReference.require_output consumes.
Backend = Pulumi Cloud or DIY. refresh syncs state from reality, explicitly. stack migrate moves between backends.

title: Configuration and Secrets
text:
Configuration and Secrets
A stack differs from its siblings in exactly two places: its state and its configuration. Configuration is how one program becomes a t3.micro in dev and a m7i.large in production without a single if. Some of that configuration is a password, and Pulumi’s secrets system makes sure the password is encrypted in every place it travels to, not just the file you typed it into.

title: Configuration and Secrets
text:
Learning goals

Set, read and structure stack configuration, and explain key namespaces
Choose between get, require and the *_secret variants, and between stack-level and project-level config
Explain how secret-ness propagates through outputs, and where it does not (resource IDs, apply callbacks)
Pick and change a secrets provider, including for DIY backends

title: Configuration and Secrets
text:
Configuration: per-stack key/value pairs
Values live in Pulumi.<stack>.yaml next to Pulumi.yaml, and you commit that file. The values drive the program, so they belong in version control alongside it.
pulumi config set aws:region us-west-2      # provider namespace
pulumi config set instanceCount 3           # project namespace (implicit)
pulumi config get instanceCount
pulumi config                               # list; --json for machines
cat id_ed25519.pub | pulumi config set publicKey   # stdin: no shell escaping
config set overwrites an existing value without warning. Review the diff of Pulumi.<stack>.yaml before committing.

Keys and namespaces
Keys are [namespace:]name. With no colon, the namespace is the project name. That is how aws:region and your own region coexist. In the stack file the result looks like:
config:
  aws:region: us-west-2
  webserver:instanceCount: "3"
In code, pulumi.Config() reads the project namespace and pulumi.Config("aws") reads another one. Reusable components should read their own namespace (pulumi.Config("mylib")) so they never collide with the consuming project.


Reading from code
import pulumi

config = pulumi.Config()
name = config.require("name")              # missing -> deployment stops with an explanatory error
count = config.get_int("instanceCount") or 1   # missing -> None, so default it
db_password = config.require_secret("dbPassword")  # Output, marked secret

aws_region = pulumi.Config("aws").require("region")
Use require for anything without a sensible default. A typo in a key should fail the preview, not quietly create one instance in production. Configuration is read-only at run time. Writing config from code is the job of the Automation API.
Environment variables also reach the program (os.environ), but configuration is per-stack, versioned and visible to collaborators, so prefer it.


Structured values
--path treats the key as a path into an object:
pulumi config set --path 'data.active' true
pulumi config set --path 'data.nums[0]' 1
pulumi config set --path 'data.nums[1]' 2
config:
  proj:data:
    active: true      # booleans stay booleans
    nums: [1, 2]      # integer-like values become integers
data = pulumi.Config().require_object("data")
active = data["active"]          # a plain dict, not a Config
require_object returns a plain dictionary. Index into it. You cannot call require on a nested value.


Project-level defaults
Values every stack shares go in Pulumi.yaml, and any stack can override them:
# Pulumi.yaml
config:
  aws:region: us-east-1
  name: BroomeLLC
  data:
    value:            # structured project-level values need this wrapper
      active: true
# Pulumi.dev.yaml: overrides for one stack
config:
  aws:region: us-east-2
  myproject:name: MopLLC
Watch the two syntaxes. The stack file uses project:key with structures nested directly. The project file uses bare key and wraps structures in value:. Project-level config is edited by hand (config set doesn’t write it) and holds plaintext only.
The project file can also type-check stack values:
config:
  name:
    type: string
    description: Base name for resources.
    default: BroomeLLC
  subnets:
    type: array
    items:
      type: string
A stack that sets name to a number then fails at pulumi preview. Type specifications don’t yet cover structured config.


Provider configuration
A provider takes settings from three places: pulumi config set aws:region ..., its environment variables, or constructor arguments. Only the default provider reads stack config. An explicit aws.Provider(...) you create reads nothing from config, so pass its arguments explicitly. To forbid implicit default providers altogether:
config:
  pulumi:disable-default-providers: ["aws", "kubernetes"]   # or ["*"]
pulumi:tags in config applies stack tags on every up or refresh. Removing a key from config does not delete the tag from the stack.

title: Configuration and Secrets
text:
Secrets

Setting
pulumi config set --secret dbPassword 'S3cr37'
The stack file now holds ciphertext:
config:
  myproject:dbPassword:
    secure: AAABAIIlW0ewSuZ1FJxw/+Rpw6BNqTUvGJ30O8WkpL2hB4aPyS7UU68=
Quote values containing $, ! or #, or pipe them from a file, so the shell doesn’t change them first. Secrets work inside structured config too: pulumi config set --path --secret 'endpoints[0].token' ....
The inverse: the CLI tries to detect values that look like tokens and stops you. When it guesses wrong, use --plaintext.
As documented (not run here), listings and accidental prints are masked:
$ pulumi config
KEY                        VALUE
aws:region                 us-west-1
dbPassword                 [secret]


Secrets are outputs that remember
A secret is an Output with a flag. Pulumi encrypts it wherever it is persisted, and propagates the flag. Anything computed from a secret with apply or Output.all is also secret. Resource properties built from it are encrypted in state.
import pulumi
import pulumi_aws as aws

cfg = pulumi.Config()
param = aws.ssm.Parameter(
    "a-secret-param",
    type="SecureString",
    value=cfg.require_secret("my-secret-value"),   # encrypted in state too
)
Ways to make a value secret:







Source
How




Config
get_secret / require_secret


An existing value
pulumi.Output.secret(value)


A resource’s outputs
ResourceOptions(additional_secret_outputs=["result"])


Derived values
Automatic via apply / Output.all on a secret



Reading a --secret key with plain require hands you the plaintext and drops the marking downstream. Always use the secret getters.


Where secret-ness ends

Inside apply. The callback receives plaintext. Pulumi marks the return value secret, but cannot stop the callback from printing or writing it to a file.
Resource IDs. A resource’s id is always stored in plaintext, and additional_secret_outputs=["id"] does nothing. random.RandomString exposes its result as its ID too, so its value lands unencrypted in state. Use random.RandomPassword and mark result secret.
Outside the stack. Secret-ness covers one stack’s state. Sharing the same credential across stacks or teams is a job for Pulumi ESC environments, which a stack imports with an environment: list in its stack file. Explicit stack config wins over imported values.



Secrets providers
By default with Pulumi Cloud, each stack gets its own Cloud-managed key and each value a nonce. Choose another provider when you use a DIY backend or your organisation mandates its own KMS:
pulumi stack init prod --secrets-provider="awskms://alias/pulumi-prod?region=us-east-1"
pulumi stack init prod --secrets-provider="gcpkms://projects/P/locations/L/keyRings/R/cryptoKeys/K"
pulumi stack init prod --secrets-provider="azurekeyvault://myvault.vault.azure.net/keys/pulumi"
pulumi stack init prod --secrets-provider="hashivault://pulumi-prod"
pulumi stack init prod --secrets-provider=passphrase

awskms accepts an ID, alias or ARN, an optional profile=, and (CLI v3.41.1+) context_<k>=<v> encryption context you can condition IAM policies on.
hashivault reads VAULT_SERVER_URL and VAULT_SERVER_TOKEN.
passphrase derives the key from a passphrase you supply (typically through PULUMI_CONFIG_PASSPHRASE). Lose it and the stack’s secrets are unrecoverable.

The provider’s public bits (encryptionsalt for passphrase, encryptedkey for KMS-style providers) are written into Pulumi.<stack>.yaml and are safe to commit. To switch an existing stack:
pulumi stack change-secrets-provider "awskms://alias/pulumi-prod?region=us-east-1"
pulumi preview      # expect: no changes
This re-encrypts config and state. If you’d rather not commit stack files at all, pulumi config refresh rebuilds them from the last deployment.

title: Configuration and Secrets
text:
Diagnosis








Symptom
Likely cause
Fix




“Missing required configuration variable”
Key not set for this stack, or wrong namespace
pulumi config -s <stack>; check the project: prefix


Value set, program says unset
Set under a different stack, or project renamed
Confirm the active stack; rename keys in the stack file


Password visible in stack export
Read with require instead of require_secret, or carried in an id
Use the secret getters; avoid ID-bearing resources


CLI refuses a harmless value as “looks like a secret”
Secret detection heuristic
--plaintext


“passphrase must be set” or decrypt fails in CI
Passphrase or KMS access missing in the runner
Provide PULUMI_CONFIG_PASSPHRASE or KMS credentials


Preview fails with a type error
Project-level type spec
Fix the stack value’s type

title: Configuration and Secrets
text:
Operational care

Commit Pulumi.yaml and Pulumi.<stack>.yaml. Ciphertext is meant to be committed. Never commit plaintext you meant to mark secret, because git history keeps it.
Treat pulumi config set in pipelines as a code change. Prefer reviewing the stack file in a PR to mutating config during deploys.
Use one KMS key or ESC environment per trust boundary (prod versus non-prod), and restrict decrypt rights accordingly.
Rotate by setting the new value with --secret and running up. Changing the provider is a separate operation (change-secrets-provider).

title: Configuration and Secrets
text:
Practice

Design config for a service with region, instance count, a list of allowed CIDRs, and a database password. Which keys go project-level, which stack-level, and which are secret?
A colleague creates a token with random.RandomString and marks result secret. What is still exposed, and what do you change?
Your team moves from Pulumi Cloud to an S3 DIY backend. What happens to secrets, and which provider would you pick?

title: Configuration and Secrets
text:
Recall card

Pulumi.<stack>.yaml holds per-stack config (commit it). Pulumi.yaml config: holds shared, plaintext, typed defaults.
No-colon keys belong to the project. Config("ns") reads other namespaces.
require fails loudly, get returns None, and *_secret keeps the marking.
Secret-ness propagates through outputs, except inside apply callbacks and resource IDs.
Use --secrets-provider at stack init and stack change-secrets-provider later. A passphrase is a key you must not lose.

title: Inputs, Outputs and the Dependency Graph
text:
Inputs, Outputs and the Dependency Graph
A Pulumi program looks imperative: Python statements, run top to bottom. The infrastructure it describes is declarative: Pulumi decides what to create, in what order, and what to leave alone. The bridge between the two is a pair of types. Inputs are what you give a resource. Outputs are values the cloud reports back later. Every confusing moment for new Pulumi users (“why does my bucket name print as an object?”) comes from treating an output as if it were already a value.

title: Inputs, Outputs and the Dependency Graph
text:
Learning goals

Distinguish inputs, resource outputs and stack outputs
Explain how passing an output into an input creates a dependency edge
Transform outputs with apply, Output.all, Output.format, Output.concat and the JSON helpers, and reach nested values by lifting
Recognise the “output used as a plain value” bug, and why resources must not be created inside apply

title: Inputs, Outputs and the Dependency Graph
text:
Inputs
An input is an argument to a resource, usually one parameter of the underlying cloud API call. Every input of type Input[T] also accepts a plain T:
import pulumi_random as random

my_id = random.RandomId("mine", byte_length=8)   # 8 is a plain value used as an input
Python offers two spellings for object-shaped inputs: an ...Args class or a dictionary typed as ...ArgsDict. Both carry the same fields, and the dictionary form is shorter:
import pulumi_aws as aws

repo = aws.ecr.Repository(
    "repo",
    image_tag_mutability="MUTABLE",
    image_scanning_configuration={"scan_on_push": True},
)

title: Inputs, Outputs and the Dependency Graph
text:
Outputs
An output is a property the provider reports after the resource exists, such as an ID, an ARN, an endpoint or a generated password. Outputs behave like futures. During a first pulumi up the value is unknown until the cloud answers. During pulumi preview it may never be known.
Pass an output straight into another resource’s input and Pulumi records a dependency:
import pulumi_aws as aws
import pulumi_random as random

password = random.RandomPassword("password", length=16, special=True)

db = aws.rds.Instance(
    "db",
    instance_class="db.t3.micro",
    allocated_storage=64,
    engine="mysql",
    username="someone",
    password=password.result,      # output -> input: an edge in the graph
)
That edge tells Pulumi to create the password before the database, and on destroy to delete the database before the password. You wrote no ordering code. A program that wires outputs to inputs gets correct ordering for free, and depends_on is only for dependencies that no value carries.
Three similar names refer to different things:







Term
What it is




Input
An argument to a resource; accepts plain values or outputs


Resource output
A property of a resource, known once the provider reports it


Stack output
A value you pulumi.export at the end of a run for the CLI or a StackReference

title: Inputs, Outputs and the Dependency Graph
text:
Getting at the value
Because an output is not yet a value, you can’t use ordinary language operations on it. print(bucket.id) or "https://" + lb.dns_name doesn’t do what you expect. The SDK supplies the tools instead.

apply: transform one output
url = lb.dns_name.apply(lambda name: f"https://{name}")
The callback runs when the value is known and receives the plain value. Its return value becomes a new Output, which you can pass on as an input or export. Secret-ness and dependencies flow through.


Output.all: combine several
import pulumi

conn = pulumi.Output.all(server.name, database.name).apply(
    lambda args: f"Server=tcp:{args[0]}.database.windows.net;initial catalog={args[1]};"
)

# keyword form yields a dict
conn = pulumi.Output.all(server=server.name, db=database.name).apply(
    lambda a: f"Server=tcp:{a['server']}.database.windows.net;initial catalog={a['db']};"
)


Helpers: skip the lambda
Most apply calls build a string or some JSON. The helpers do that directly and are easier to read:
import json
import pulumi

url = pulumi.Output.format("https://{0}/api", lb.dns_name)
arn_path = pulumi.Output.concat(bucket.arn, "/*")

policy = pulumi.Output.json_dumps({
    "Version": "2012-10-17",
    "Statement": [{
        "Effect": "Allow",
        "Principal": "*",
        "Action": ["s3:GetObject"],
        "Resource": [arn_path],          # outputs allowed inside the structure
    }],
})

parsed = pulumi.Output.json_loads(some_json_output)
json_dumps accepts a structure that has outputs nested inside it. A json.dumps inside an apply would make you resolve each one by hand first.


Lifting: reach into nested outputs
Properties and indexes can be read straight off an output, with no apply. Pulumi “lifts” the access:
record_name = cert.domain_validation_options[0].resource_record_name
Without lifting this would be cert.domain_validation_options.apply(lambda o: o[0].resource_record_name).

title: Inputs, Outputs and the Dependency Graph
section: Two rules that prevent most bugs
text:
Two rules that prevent most bugs
1. Never treat an output as a plain value. Printing it, concatenating it with +, using it in an if, or formatting it with an f-string outside apply gives you the wrapper object, not the value. Python’s Output warns when converted to a string, and the result ends up in resource names and tags looking like garbage. Use apply, format, concat or json_dumps.
2. Don’t create resources inside apply or all. Pulumi’s documentation says to avoid it wherever possible. Resources created in a callback don’t appear in pulumi preview unless the value is already known, so the preview stops matching what up will do. Reviewers then approve a plan that leaves things out. If the number of resources depends on a value, read that value from configuration (known at preview), not from another resource’s output.

title: Inputs, Outputs and the Dependency Graph
text:
Resource identity
Wiring resources means passing some identifier, and the inputs differ in which one they want. A resource has four identities: its logical name (the first constructor argument), its physical name at the provider, its physical ID (resource.id), and its Pulumi URN. Many inputs want an ARN, an endpoint or a name instead of the ID. A type mismatch at preview usually means you passed the wrong identity. Check the input’s documentation.

Symptom
Cause
Fix

Resources created inside apply
Drive counts from config. Create resources at top level


Resources created in the wrong order
The dependency is not carried by any value
Pass the output as an input, or depends_on as a last resort

Passed the resource, not a property
bucket.id, bucket.arn or bucket.bucket, per the input’s docs

title: Inputs, Outputs and the Dependency Graph
text:
Practice

Build an output URL https://<dns>/health from a load balancer’s dns_name three ways: apply, Output.format and Output.concat. Which reads best?
A colleague loops for i in range(int(count_output)). Explain why this fails and rewrite it to use config.
Write an S3 bucket policy that references two buckets’ ARNs, using only Output.json_dumps.

title: Inputs, Outputs and the Dependency Graph
text:
Recall card

Inputs accept plain values or outputs. Outputs are future values reported by the provider.
Output to input means a dependency edge. Ordering for create and destroy is automatic.
apply handles one output, Output.all several, and format/concat/json_dumps/json_loads are the common shortcuts. Lifting reads nested fields.
Never treat an output as plain, and never create resources inside apply.
